pages.text: A lantern swings up the road in the daylight. Under it walks Pieter, the night watchman. He does not look happy.
“I am sorry, {player}. The Lord wants his share. It is not my idea. I only carry the book.” He shows you a number. “Pay when you can. I will wait at the gate.”

You bring a big pot to the Hall: leeks and beans and your own bread. The soup in the Pot goes thick, and the whole village goes quiet, tasting. At your gate, when Pieter comes, there is a stool you made yourself. Three legs. It wobbles only slightly.

“Sit,” you say. “After you,” says Pieter. “It's for you.” “I couldn't sit while you're standing.” Then the bunny hops up onto the stool and sits in the middle, ears flat. So you both eat on the ground, with the bunny above you on her throne.

Sitting down, Pieter looks much older. He eats every drop. Then he taps his book shut. “Thank you. Most people hide when they see me coming.” He almost smiles. Then he walks home, whistling a tune he does not know he is whistling.

c3_k_pieter.text: Far down the road, a lantern waves at you. Pieter. You wave back.

pages.text: Another letter comes from the river barge. Your mother writes: “Stay if you must. Your cousin asks after you.” You read the last line again.

Your cousin. Liv. Four years older, thin and sharp, always watching, with eyes that missed nothing, ever. Liv was always in the loft, looking out of the little window. To anyone else it would sound like a kind line. To you it sounds like a warning.

c3_miller.title: The miller on the bridge
c3_miller.text: On the bridge, the miller glares down at the stream. It is still very low. He glares at you, too, just in case.

pages.text: Old Odinson lights the forge and young Bo works the bellows. They show you how to hold the tongs. “Good hands,” says Odinson, which is the most he has said all day. Bo grins at the fire.

When Odinson is out of earshot, Bo says, “I carried a bucket that night, in the line. I was little.” He hammers a nail. “Somebody gave me theirs. Bigger than mine. It was empty.” He looks at you, then at the nail. “Yeah.”
In the old mill, on a rusty nail, hangs a bell. It is far too small for a cow. It is far too small for anything. It sways, just a little, though there is no wind.
In the dust beneath it you think you see tiny footprints. You look the other way. You are quite sure that you looked the other way.

On the plaster is a charcoal drawing: a child with a bucket nearly as big as the child, holding hands with something the size of a thumb. You do not remember drawing it. You find you are humming, and you go out very fast.

The stream runs clear again, all the way down to Hazelwood. On the bridge by his mill the miller looks down. The water is high and quick and brown, and his old wheel is going round, creaking and splashing. He looks at you. He nods once, a very small nod. That is his whole apology, and you take it.

“Thank you,” says the miller, fast, glaring hard at the stream. “Now I owe the Hurst a penny a sack again.” You laugh out loud on the bridge. Then you stop. A penny a sack. Every good thing you do down here, the Lord takes a piece of.

c3_dance.title: The harvest dance
c3_dance.text: You work the cider while the village dances. Mugs float above the heads. One falls, you catch it, and you laugh out loud. Somewhere close by, something goes tink, like a very small bell. You do not look.

pages.text: A goat trots up the path and straight into the brambles nobody could clear. Crunch. Munch. She eats thistles as if they were sweets. You open your mouth to stop her. Then you let her.
The third line of the old rhyme comes back, and you say it with your mouth still open: “Brave goat clears the bramble bed.” The goat looks at your hat. Her eyes are thoughtful.
In the morning the scarecrow is wearing your green hat, high up, out of reach of goats, at a very jaunty angle. Nobody saw who put it there.

Tucked into the band is a letter from Mei. “Your cousin asked me three times whether she might come up to your gate. I told her to ask you herself. She said she was asking.” You take your hat back. It is still warm.

c3_frame3.title: Back in the room
c3_frame3.text: “Were you scared of the cousin?” asks somebody from under a blanket. “More than of any imp,” you say. “What's an imp?” “Shh!” say three children at once. “That comes later!”

c3_k_count_sheep.text: You try to count the sheep. They keep swapping places. You get three, then five, then you nearly fall asleep.
